source.title: Video Parallel Scaling: Aggregating Diverse Frame Subsets for VideoLLMs
source.authors: Hyungjin Chung; Hyelin Nam; Jiyeon Kim; Hyojun Go; Byeongjun Park; Junho Kim; Joonseok Lee; Seongsu Ha; Byung-Hoon Kim

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendix are present; no material cutoff or document mismatch is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling-law analysis to VideoLLMs and derives conditional cross-entropy expressions for video-frame subsets and parallel streams. It does not empirically fit or test pretraining-loss scaling curves.
record.gate_note: The relevant result is a theoretical derivation for VideoLLM cross-entropy loss in Appendix A. The experiments report benchmark accuracy and other scores for VPS as stream count, frame count, model, and sampling strategy vary; they do not report held-out cross-entropy loss or fit loss-scaling curves, so those benchmark results are not rows for the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The paper assumes a simplified Chinchilla law, L(N)=E+A/N^α, and derives from it an approximate loss for VPS. It measures no loss and fits no curve. Its experiments report benchmark accuracy for its own inference-time method (VPS) on off-the-shelf models. The scaling law is used as a tool, not tested, so this is T4.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors argue theoretically, assuming a simplified Chinchilla law, that VPS 'contracts the Chinchilla scaling law' when streams use uncorrelated frame subsets. Empirically, VPS improves accuracy across Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3 and Gemma3 (2B–32B). It also scales better than Self-consistency and complements TCD and RITUAL. The scaling-law claim is a derivation, not a measured result.
record.recipe_differences: The paper derives a video-specific theoretical expression based on a simplified Chinchilla law and evaluates inference-time parallel frame aggregation; it does not reproduce the original training-loss scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: In the VPS benchmark experiments, reported accuracy varies with stream count, frame count, model, video duration, and frame-sampling strategy. These are not cross-entropy scaling measurements.

fits_no_version.finding: Accuracy on EventHallusion and Video-MME generally rises with the number of parallel inference streams J (1, 2, 4, 8) using disjoint frame subsets. The paper says gains are larger for bigger models and longer videos (Fig. 2, 3, 4, 5; Tab. 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling inference-time parallel streams over diverse inputs improves downstream accuracy of VideoLLMs (inference-time parallel scaling), distinct from pretraining loss scaling.

record.peer_reviewed: 2026 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition - Findings Track (CVPRF)
record.problems: The relevant loss result is theoretical and assumes a simplified Chinchilla law; no empirical held-out cross-entropy results or fitted scaling exponents are reported. The paper's benchmark experiments use accuracy and other output metrics rather than loss.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Benchmark accuracy and free-form response scores for VPS are not cross-entropy scaling results or tests of the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: No measured held-out loss across parameters, tokens or compute.
No comparison of shape at a fixed parameter count.
No empirical loss scaling in video or multimodal models. The power-law form is assumed, not measured.
Accuracy is reported for models from 2B to 32B across different families, but there is no test of predictability from scale or loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labelled this T3 with a limits_scope verdict on V5 based on the theoretical derivation. That is wrong: a derivation that presupposes the law cannot test it. The reader's own gate_note and untested_parts already state that no loss is measured. All labels are removed.

versions.untested_parts: No empirical held-out pretraining-loss sweep over parameter count, training tokens, or compute; the paper's analysis assumes a simplified parameter-count scaling law.
No small-run fits or predictions evaluated against much larger runs.
No fixed training-compute budget comparison or loss-minimising allocation between parameters and training tokens.
Although several VideoLLM architectures are evaluated, the study does not compare loss at fixed parameter count while varying architecture details.
The paper derives a conditional expression for VideoLLM loss, but does not empirically measure or fit cross-entropy scaling in video models, and does not test other modalities or training regimes.
Benchmark outcomes are reported, but the study does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss or a fitted scaling relation.
No comparison of fitted exponents or allocation trends across counting, schedule, data, or fitting choices.

rows.subject: VideoLLM
rows.size_stated: N parameters; particular size not stated
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical derivation of cross-entropy loss for a VideoLLM receiving a subset of video frames

conditions.value: single stream; subset of video frames

rows.value: L_j(N) = E + A/N^α + B_j + O(B_j^2) + O(Δ_j^3)
rows.locator: Appendix A, Proposition 1, Eq. 23; related discussion in Sec. 3.2
rows.note: This is a theoretical expression, not a measured loss curve. The additional B_j term represents bias from seeing only a subset of frames.
rows.check: This is a theoretical expression derived by assuming the simplified Chinchilla law (App. A, Eq. 23), not a measured result. It cannot bear on whether the power-law form holds for video models. 'Partial' is not justified.

rows.subject: VideoLLM
rows.size_stated: N parameters; particular size not stated
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical derivation of expected loss when aggregating predictions from J parallel streams using different frame subsets
rows.baseline: Single-stream subset loss: E + A/N^α + B_j, up to higher-order terms
rows.locator: Appendix A, Proposition 1, Eq. 24; related discussion in Sec. 3.2
rows.note: The derived expression retains parameter-count power-law dependence under the stated assumptions, while including frame-subset bias and a residual-correlation term. It is theoretical, not an empirical validation of a video loss-scaling curve.
rows.check: This is a theoretical derivation for VPS loss (Eq. 24) that takes the Chinchilla law as a premise and adapts the ParScale lemma. No empirical loss is reported, so it is not evidence for V5. The 'partial' state is unfounded.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Theoretical VideoLLM analysis with frame subsets; simplified Chinchilla law assumed
reader_labels.reason: The derivation gives a conditional parameter-count power-law form but includes additional frame-subset bias and correlation terms, and the paper reports no empirical video cross-entropy scaling fit (r1, r2).
